message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of work:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from your OS to office apps. | Specialized for parallel tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, AI, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with deep pipelines, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores arranged in many small “threads” that can run the same instruction on many data points simultaneously. |
| **Execution Model** | *Serial* / *few‑threaded*: one core does a few instructions at a time, but it can switch context quickly. | *Massively parallel*: thousands of lightweight threads execute the same code over large data sets. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory interface, supports complex addressing and caching policies. | Smaller per‑core cache; relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory spaces. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Branch‑heavy, irregular, low‑latency tasks (e.g., running an OS, web browsing, word processing). | Data‑parallel, compute‑intensive workloads (e.g., matrix multiplication, image filtering, machine‑learning inference). |
| **Programming Models** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with thread libraries like pthreads, OpenMP. | Parallel programming models like CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan, Metal, or higher‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |
| **Power & Cost** | Lower power per core, cheaper to produce per core. | Higher power density, more expensive per core, but cost per FLOP is lower when you need massive throughput. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Latency vs Throughput**: CPUs excel at low latency (quickly finishing a single task), GPUs excel at throughput (finishing many similar tasks quickly).
- **Instruction Set Complexity**: CPUs have richer instruction sets (more addressing modes, SIMD extensions like AVX/NEON) whereas GPUs use simpler, highly optimized instruction sets tailored for vector operations.
- **Use Cases**: If you’re building a game engine, you’ll use the GPU for rendering and the CPU for physics, AI decision making, and I/O. In machine learning training, the GPU’s parallelism dramatically speeds up tensor operations.

In short, think of the CPU as a versatile multitasker and the GPU as a specialized factory line that can process many identical items at once.
